authority: NSSCAS Examiners Report 2025, Chemistry 8224 Papers 1-3. Only examiner-report evidence held for this subject; 2021-2024 reports do not exist.
derivation_policy: Curated by hand from the located examiner statements and restated in our words. Slips, answering habits (for example citing parallax or human error as an experimental error), item-specific mistakes and items where the report states only the correct answer were left out. No report wording appears in learner-facing output.
how_to_use: Every entry earns one MISCON card on its objective: the error, the correct idea, and the test that tells them apart. Each is single-source (one report, one series), so under the two-source rule agreed for this run it needs a second source before it publishes as examiner-evidenced.

kinds.adjacent_concept: Two different concepts that sit near each other in the syllabus.
kinds.near_neighbour_term: Two similar terms or values confused.
kinds.wrong_angle_same_concept: The right concept approached or applied the wrong way.

entries.objective_text: perform calculations, including use of the mole concept, involving: - reacting masses (from formulae and equations) - volumes of gases at r.t.p and s.t.p (e.g. in the burning of hydrocarbons) - volumes and concentrations of solutions NOTE:
entries.a: Using the r.t.p. molar gas volume (24 dm3 mol-1) in a calculation set at s.t.p.
entries.b: The molar gas volume is 22.4 dm3 mol-1 at s.t.p. and 24.0 dm3 mol-1 at r.t.p.; the conditions the question states decide which value to use.
entries.test: Does the question say s.t.p. or r.t.p.?
entries.evidence_strength: stated by the examiner report; single series; question paper not held

entries.objective_text: analyse mass spectra in terms of isotopic abundances (knowledge of the working of the mass spectrometer is not required)
entries.a: Counting the peaks in the mass spectrum of Cl2 as the number of chlorine isotopes.
entries.b: Peaks of a diatomic element's spectrum include molecular ions made from different isotope combinations, so there are more peaks than isotopes; the isotopes are found by working out which combinations produce each peak.
entries.test: Is this peak one atom's ion or an ion of a molecule made from two atoms?
entries.evidence_strength: stated by the examiner report; single series; question paper not held

entries.objective_text: calculate the relative atomic mass of an element given the relative abundances of its isotopes, or its mass spectrum
entries.a: Dividing the sum of (mass x peak height) by 100 when the peak heights are not percentages.
entries.b: A weighted mean divides by the total of the weights; that total is 100 only when the heights are already percentages.
entries.test: Do the peak heights add up to 100?
entries.evidence_strength: stated by the examiner report; single series; question paper not held

entries.objective_text: identify and describe protons, neutrons and electrons in terms of their relative charges and relative masses
entries.a: Giving the electron a relative mass of 0, or 'nil' for a neutron, as if mass and charge were the same thing.
entries.b: Relative mass: proton 1, neutron 1, electron about 1/1836 (very small but not zero). Relative charge: proton +1, neutron 0, electron -1.
entries.test: Is the table column asking about mass or charge?
entries.evidence_strength: stated by the examiner report; single series; question paper not held

entries.objective_text: identify and describe protons, neutrons and electrons in terms of their relative charges and relative masses
entries.a: Drawing electrons and protons deflected by the same amount in an electric field.
entries.b: Electron and proton carry charges of equal size but opposite sign, and the electron's mass is far smaller, so it is deflected much more and towards the other plate; neutrons are not deflected. (The syllabus names behaviour in electric fields only in the general objective of 1.2.1.)
entries.test: Which particle has the smaller mass for the same size of charge?
entries.evidence_strength: stated by the examiner report; single series; question paper not held

entries.objective_text: state the electronic configuration of atoms and ions given the proton (atomic) number and charge, using the convention 1s22s22p6, etc, and electrons in boxes representation, for example: oxygen
entries.a: Writing chromium as 3d4 4s2, following the simple filling order.
entries.b: The ground-state configuration of chromium is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d5 4s1: a half-filled 3d sub-shell with one 4s electron.
entries.test: Does the configuration follow the filling order, or the known exception for Cr?
entries.evidence_strength: stated by the examiner report; single series; question paper not held

entries.objective_text: recall the number of orbitals making up s-, p- and d- sub-shells, and the number of electrons that can fill s-,p- and d-sub-shells
entries.a: Giving how many electrons the s, p and d sub-shells hold when asked how many orbitals of each type are occupied.
entries.b: Count orbitals, not electrons: an s sub-shell is 1 orbital, a p sub-shell 3 and a d sub-shell 5, and each holds up to 2 electrons.
entries.test: Is the question about orbitals or electrons?
entries.evidence_strength: stated by the examiner report; single series; question paper not held

entries.objective_text: use oxidation numbers to name oxyanions, including nitrate(III) NO2-, nitrate(V) NO3-, chlorate(I) ClO-, chlorate(V) ClO3-
entries.a: Naming NO2- as nitrate(V) because nitrate is the familiar oxyanion of nitrogen.
entries.b: Name an oxyanion from the oxidation number you calculate: nitrogen in NO2- is +3, so it is nitrate(III); NO3- is nitrate(V).
entries.test: What oxidation number does nitrogen have in this ion?
entries.evidence_strength: stated by the examiner report; single series; question paper not held

entries.objective_text: explain, in terms of electronegativity, the properties of molecules such as bond polarity the dipole moments of molecules and the behaviour of oxides with water
entries.a: Treating hydrogen chloride as an ionic compound.
entries.b: Hydrogen chloride is a covalent molecule with a polar bond: the electrons are shared unequally, not transferred.
entries.test: Are electrons shared (unequally) or transferred from one atom to the other?
entries.evidence: 2025 report, Paper 1 Q8 (67% correct; option C most chosen error)
entries.evidence_strength: stated by the examiner report; single series; question paper not held

entries.objective_text: describe the differences between bonding (intramolecular) and intermolecular forces in covalent molecules
entries.a: Calling van der Waals forces (or other intermolecular forces) 'bonds' when asked for the bonding in a covalent substance.
entries.b: Bonding is what holds atoms together inside a molecule or lattice (covalent bonds in SO2); intermolecular forces act between molecules and are weaker.
entries.test: Does the force act inside the molecule or between molecules?
entries.evidence_strength: stated by the examiner report; single series; question paper not held

entries.objective_text: explain and use the term activation energy, including reference to the Boltzmann distribution
entries.a: Drawing a reaction-pathway (energy profile) diagram when asked for a Boltzmann distribution curve.
entries.b: A Boltzmann curve plots number of molecules against energy; an energy profile plots energy against progress of reaction.
entries.test: What is on the vertical axis: number of molecules or energy?
entries.evidence_strength: stated by the examiner report; single series; question paper not held

entries.objective_text: explain and use the term activation energy, including reference to the Boltzmann distribution
entries.a: Saying the area under the right-hand part of the curve is the activation energy.
entries.b: Activation energy is a value on the energy axis; the area beyond it represents the fraction of molecules with energy at least equal to Ea.
entries.test: Is Ea a position on the axis or an area under the curve?
entries.evidence_strength: stated by the examiner report; single series; question paper not held

entries.objective_text: explain qualitatively, in terms both of the Boltzmann distribution and of collision frequency, the effect of temperature change on the rate of a reaction
entries.a: Explaining the faster rate at a higher temperature only as 'collisions are more frequent'.
entries.b: A higher temperature raises collision frequency, and also the proportion of molecules with energy at least Ea, so many more collisions are successful.
entries.test: Have you said more collisions or more successful collisions, and why?
entries.evidence_strength: stated by the examiner report; single series; question paper not held

entries.objective_text: explain the importance of choice of conditions (temperature, pressure, use of a catalyst) for processes used in the chemical industry including the Haber process and the Contact process, in terms of equilibrium (yield) and rate
entries.a: Justifying an industrial temperature by yield alone or by rate alone.
entries.b: For an exothermic equilibrium process, a lower temperature favours the yield and a higher one speeds the reaction; the chosen temperature is a compromise between both.
entries.test: Have you discussed both rate and yield at the chosen temperature?
entries.evidence_strength: stated by the examiner report; single series; question paper not held

entries.objective_text: state and explain the variation in oxidation number of the oxides (sodium to sulfur only) and chlorides (sodium to phosphorus only) in terms of their valence shell electrons
entries.a: Saying the maximum oxidation number of the Period 3 oxides rises and then falls across the period.
entries.b: Across the oxides from sodium to sulfur (the range the syllabus names) the oxidation number of the element rises from +1 to +6, matching the number of valence electrons used.
entries.test: Compare the oxidation number in Na2O, MgO, Al2O3, SiO2, P4O10 and SO3: does it ever fall?
entries.evidence_strength: stated by the examiner report; single series; question paper not held

entries.objective_text: recall the chemistry of alcohols, exemplified by ethanol, in the following reactions: - combustion - substitution to give halogenoalkanes - reaction with sodium - oxidation to carbonyl compounds and carboxylic acids - dehydration to alkenes
entries.a: Naming dilute acid as the reagent to dehydrate an alcohol to an alkene.
entries.b: Dehydration of an alcohol needs concentrated acid (or a hot catalyst); dilute acid supplies water and favours the reverse, hydration.
entries.test: Is the acid concentrated or dilute?
entries.evidence_strength: stated by the examiner report; single series; question paper not held

entries.objective_text: deduce the presence of a CH3CH(OH)– group in an alcohol from its reaction with alkaline aqueous iodine to form tri-iodomethane
entries.a: Describing a positive alkaline iodine test as a colour change in solution.
entries.b: A positive alkaline iodine test gives a pale yellow precipitate (tri-iodomethane).
entries.test: Does the result describe a precipitate or only a colour change?
entries.evidence_strength: stated by the examiner report; single series; question paper not held

entries.objective_text: deduce the presence of a CH3CH(OH)– group in an alcohol from its reaction with alkaline aqueous iodine to form tri-iodomethane
entries.a: Naming an iodoalkane such as iodobutane as the compound that forms in the alkaline iodine test.
entries.b: The yellow solid formed is tri-iodomethane, CHI3, produced from the CH3CH(OH)- group; the alcohol is not turned into an iodoalkane.
entries.test: Which group in the alcohol reacts, and what does it become?
entries.evidence_strength: stated by the examiner report; single series; question paper not held

entries.objective_text: deduce the repeat unit of an addition polymer obtained from a given monomer
entries.a: Drawing the repeat unit of an addition polymer with the C=C double bond still in it.
entries.b: In addition polymerisation the double bond is used up: the repeat unit is saturated, with a bond extending out of each end.
entries.test: Does the repeat unit still contain C=C?
entries.evidence_strength: stated by the examiner report; single series; question paper not held
